chapter.title: The Unfinished Footstep
chapter.body:
The footstep lands beautifully, which is the trouble.

You have brought it forward beneath the scrape of a chair, softened its edge and given it enough space to suggest someone entering. Then the recording continues, and nobody does anything. There is no performer to take over. Your headphones deliver the faint room noise with embarrassing fidelity.

At the kitchen table after work, you move the footstep back. Now it sounds like someone leaving. That is worse: the whole piece seems to have happened before you pressed play.

February goes into endings. You build a low rumble from the chair legs, let it swell, listen, remove it. You try returning to the opening scrape. The neatness makes you wince. Administration fills the working day; on an evening when you can barely distinguish one version from another, you close the editor rather than export another near-identical file. The vacancy you declined passes its deadline without an application.

By March, the source recording has become familiar enough that you know where a voice will enter before you hear it. You leave those passages out. What remains is less sociable than the room was: wood dragging, weight shifting, footsteps approaching a microphone that nobody is attending to.

You begin leaving more space between them.

The gaps are awkward. You reach for the volume control, certain playback has stopped, and a scrape arrives while your hand is still moving. For once, you let that happen again without shortening the gap.

At the end, you cut into a returning footstep before its weight settles. Your body supplies the missing landing. You dislike how abruptly the room disappears. You restore the landing, listen through, and hear the familiar preparation for an entrance. You remove it again.

You export the piece as Four Minutes After Clearing. The source stays separate. Listening to the finished file, away from the coloured blocks of the editor, you catch yourself anticipating the long middle silence with pleasure. The ending still catches at you. You keep it.

For a while, finishing is enough. Spring passes around ordinary working days, and the composition remains unchanged.

On a wet afternoon in June, Tunde comes into the kitchen carrying a plate. Your laptop, cable and notebook occupy the place where he wants to sit.

“Can I have the table?”

“Yes. Let me save this.”

Before closing the session, you click a chair scrape you have isolated from the source. On its own it gives a short, rubbery squawk. You play it again.

Tunde looks at the speaker, then at you.

“Was that meant to happen?”

“It was a chair.”

“Fine. Can the chair move?”

You lift the laptop, laughing, and catch the cable against your wrist before it drags his fork off the table. He sets his plate down in the cleared space. You take the work elsewhere.

Without the slow approach you gave it in the composition, the scrape sounds ridiculous. You trim away the surrounding room noise and export it separately. Then you isolate a footfall, a small wooden knock, a longer drag. Each starts before you have time to settle into an atmosphere. You keep playing them in abrupt succession, pleased by their bluntness.

In July, preparing a release means listening closely again. You make a local folder for the finished piece and another for the selected fragments. Nothing has been uploaded. The title looks unexpectedly formal beside your name.

You play the composition all the way through. During the long gap, you can hear traffic outside your own room; then the recorded footsteps return, and the two spaces separate. You remember exactly why you left that silence alone.

Next you rearrange the fragments. The knock comes first, the scrape answers, and the footfall blunders in too late. You laugh aloud. You repeat the sequence to check that it was funny, and spoil it by anticipating the interruption.

There is a place in the release notes for permission. You type a sentence allowing the fragments to be used in other work, then mark it as a draft. It looks small beside the effort of making the files. Someone could follow it without ever hearing the composition.

You had enjoyed making the room solemn. You enjoyed making it ridiculous, too. Now you find yourself protective of a chair scrape.

Let me save this.”"},{"index":14,"text":"Before closing the session, you click a chair scrape you have isolated from the source. On its own it gives a short, rubbery squawk. You play it again."},{"index":15,"text":"Tunde looks at the speaker, then at you."},{"index":16,"text":"“Was that meant to happen?”"},{"index":17,"text":"“It was a chair.”"},{"index":18,"text":"“Fine. Can the chair move?”"},{"index":19,"text":"You lift the laptop, laughing, and catch the cable against your wrist before it drags his fork off the table. He sets his plate down in the cleared space. You take the work elsewhere."},{"index":20,"text":"Without the slow approach you gave it in the composition, the scrape sounds ridiculous. You keep playing them in abrupt succession, pleased by their bluntness."},{"index":21,"text":"In July, preparing a release means listening closely again. You remember exactly why you left that silence alone."},{"index":23,"text":"Next you rearrange the fragments. The knock comes first, the scrape answers, and the footfall blunders in too late.
